claim: Three-photon excitation has recently been demonstrated as an effective method to perform intravital microscopy in deep, previously inaccessible regions of the mouse brain.
source: Three-photon excitation has recently been demonstrated as an effective method to perform intravital microscopy in deep, previously inaccessible regions of the mouse brain.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript and likely by citations in the full text.

claim: High-pulse-energy 1 MHz pulse-repetition-rate infrared excitation near 1300 and 1700 nm provides a more than 2-fold increased imaging depth in tumor and bone tissue compared to illumination conditions commonly used in 2-photon excitation.
source: We show that this excitation regime provides a more than 2-fold increased imaging depth in tumor and bone tissue compared to the illumination conditions commonly used in 2-photon excitation, due to improved excitation confinement and reduced scattering.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including SNR analysis and imaging depth measurements shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The increased imaging depth is due to improved excitation confinement and reduced scattering.
source: We show that this excitation regime provides a more than 2-fold increased imaging depth in tumor and bone tissue compared to the illumination conditions commonly used in 2-photon excitation, due to improved excitation confinement and reduced scattering.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, supported by measurements of effective attenuation length and resolution analysis.

claim: Simultaneous 3- and 4-photon processes can be effectively induced with a single laser line.
source: We also show that simultaneous 3- and 4-photon processes can be effectively induced with a single laser line, enabling the combined detection of blue to far-red fluorescence together with second and third harmonic generation without chromatic aberration, at excitation intensities compatible with live tissue imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through power-dependence measurements shown in Figure 1d and multicolor imaging in Figure 1b-c.

claim: Single laser line excitation enables combined detection of blue to far-red fluorescence together with second and third harmonic generation without chromatic aberration.
source: We also show that simultaneous 3- and 4-photon processes can be effectively induced with a single laser line, enabling the combined detection of blue to far-red fluorescence together with second and third harmonic generation without chromatic aberration, at excitation intensities compatible with live tissue imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiparametric imaging experiments shown in Figure 1b-c.

claim: The excitation intensities used are compatible with live tissue imaging.
source: We also show that simultaneous 3- and 4-photon processes can be effectively induced with a single laser line, enabling the combined detection of blue to far-red fluorescence together with second and third harmonic generation without chromatic aberration, at excitation intensities compatible with live tissue imaging.
evidence: This is supported by phototoxicity experiments shown in Figure 2, which establish safe imaging thresholds.

claim: Photoperturbation thresholds have been analyzed for this excitation regime.
source: Finally, we analyze photoperturbation thresholds in this excitation regime and derive setpoints for safe cell imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic phototoxicity experiments using GCaMP6 and Sytox reporters shown in Figure 2.

claim: Setpoints for safe cell imaging have been derived.
source: Finally, we analyze photoperturbation thresholds in this excitation regime and derive setpoints for safe cell imaging.
evidence: Safe imaging thresholds are established as 2.8 nJ for 1300 nm and 8.7 nJ for 1650 nm excitation, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Infrared high-pulse-energy low-repetition-rate excitation opens novel perspectives for intravital deep-tissue microscopy of multiple parameters in strongly scattering tissues and organs.
source: Together, these results indicate that infrared high-pulse-energy low-repetition-rate excitation opens novel perspectives for intravital deep-tissue microscopy of multiple parameters in strongly scattering tissues and organs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Confocal microscopy enables a penetration depth less than 100 µm.
source: Linear imaging modalities such as confocal microscopy enable a penetration depth less than 100 µm (Helmchen and Denk, 2005), which restricts their application to low-scattering, thin or surface-specific tissue models, such as the mouse inner ear and chick embryo (Deryugina, 2016; Tomo et al., 2007; Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Helmchen and Denk, 2005.

claim: Confocal microscopy is restricted to low-scattering, thin or surface-specific tissue models.
source: Linear imaging modalities such as confocal microscopy enable a penetration depth less than 100 µm (Helmchen and Denk, 2005), which restricts their application to low-scattering, thin or surface-specific tissue models, such as the mouse inner ear and chick embryo (Deryugina, 2016; Tomo et al., 2007; Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deryugina, 2016 and Tomo et al., 2007.

claim: 2-photon microscopy based on high-frequency near-infrared excitation pulses (80 MHz, ~100–200 fs, 800–1300 nm) provides 100–400 µm imaging depth in highly scattering tissues.
source: Taking advantage of reduced scattering and absorption of the excitation light and selective excitation of the focal plane (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Diaspro et al., 2005), 2-photon (2P) microscopy based on high-frequency near-infrared excitation pulses (80 MHz, ~100–200 fs, 800–1300 nm, further referred to as lowIR) provides 100–400 µm imaging depth in highly scattering tissues, for example, liver (Ritsma et al., 2012) and skin (Andresen et al., 2009), and up to 500–800 µm in less scattering tissues, such as mouse brain cortex (Helmchen and Denk, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ritsma et al., 2012 and Andresen et al., 2009.

claim: 2-photon microscopy provides up to 500–800 µm imaging depth in less scattering tissues, such as mouse brain cortex.
source: Taking advantage of reduced scattering and absorption of the excitation light and selective excitation of the focal plane (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Diaspro et al., 2005), 2-photon (2P) microscopy based on high-frequency near-infrared excitation pulses (80 MHz, ~100–200 fs, 800–1300 nm, further referred to as lowIR) provides 100–400 µm imaging depth in highly scattering tissues, for example, liver (Ritsma et al., 2012) and skin (Andresen et al., 2009), and up to 500–800 µm in less scattering tissues, such as mouse brain cortex (Helmchen and Denk, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Helmchen and Denk, 2005.

claim: Efficient 3P microscopy requires shorter (sub-100 fs) pulses at the focus with ~5–10 times higher energy compared to 2P microscopy.
source: In contrast to the well-established 2P microscopy lowIR excitation regime (100–200 fs pulses with sub-nJ energy density at the focus), efficient 3P microscopy requires shorter (sub-100 fs) pulses at the focus with ~5–10 times higher energy (König et al., 1999) (highIR excitation) to generate comparable excitation of fluorophores (Xu et al., 1996; Wang and Xu, 2020; Supplementary file 1a, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to König et al., 1999, Xu et al., 1996, and Wang and Xu, 2020.

claim: 3P microscopy applies lower pulse repetition rates (1–2 MHz) compared to pulse repetition rates commonly used for 2P microscopy (80 MHz) to keep average power and sample heating at acceptable levels.
source: To keep the average power and associated sample heating at an acceptable level, 3P microscopy applies lower pulse repetition rates (1–2 MHz) compared to pulse repetition rates commonly used for 2P microscopy (80 MHz) (Beaurepaire et al., 2001; Theer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaurepaire et al., 2001 and Theer et al., 2003.

claim: The setup achieved a resolution better than 0.8 µm in the lateral and 3 µm in the axial dimension.
source: Excitation was focused with a high-NA objective, resulting in a resolution better than 0.8 µm in the lateral and 3 µm in the axial dimension (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1650 nm highIR excitation enables resolution of structural details with THG contrast at depths encompassing the entire cortex (>1 mm) in mouse brain.
source: Using the mouse brain as a reference (Horton et al., 2013; Weisenburger et al., 2019), we confirmed that 1650 nm highIR excitation enables to resolve structural details with third harmonic generation (THG) contrast at depths encompassing the entire cortex (>1 mm), which outperforms the imaging depth obtained with 1270 nm lowIR excitation by almost a factor of two (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b,c.

claim: 1650 nm highIR excitation outperforms 1270 nm lowIR excitation by almost a factor of two in imaging depth in mouse brain.
source: Using the mouse brain as a reference (Horton et al., 2013; Weisenburger et al., 2019), we confirmed that 1650 nm highIR excitation enables to resolve structural details with third harmonic generation (THG) contrast at depths encompassing the entire cortex (>1 mm), which outperforms the imaging depth obtained with 1270 nm lowIR excitation by almost a factor of two (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b,c.

claim: In the neocortex, the effective attenuation length (le) was 336 µm for 1650 nm excitation and 280 µm for 1280 nm excitation.
source: In the neocortex, le was 336 µm for 1650 nm excitation and 280 µm for 1280 nm excitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), in agreement with previous work (Horton et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: When excited at 1650 nm, TagRFP, mCherry, and AF680 followed a cubic dependence on excitation power, consistent with third-order processes.
source: When excited at 1650 nm, the red fluorophores TagRFP, mCherry, and AF680 followed a cubic dependence on excitation power, while green and blue fluorophores eGFP and Hoechst followed a quartic dependence, consistent with respective third- and fourth-order processes (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by power-dependence measurements shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: When excited at 1650 nm, eGFP and Hoechst followed a quartic dependence on excitation power, consistent with fourth-order processes.
source: When excited at 1650 nm, the red fluorophores TagRFP, mCherry, and AF680 followed a cubic dependence on excitation power, while green and blue fluorophores eGFP and Hoechst followed a quartic dependence, consistent with respective third- and fourth-order processes (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by power-dependence measurements shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: 3- and 4-photon-excited fluorescence along with multi-harmonic SHG and THG signals were obtained simultaneously using 1650 nm excitation, resulting in six-channel images in a single scan.
source: This shows that 3- and 4-photon-excited fluorescence (3PEF, 4PEF) along with multi-harmonic SHG and THG signals were obtained simultaneously using 1650 nm excitation, resulting in six-channel images in a single scan (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiparametric imaging shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A key advantage of one-shot excitation scheme is that it is free of chromatic aberration.
source: Although independent control of each respective signal strength is not possible, a key advantage of this one-shot excitation scheme is that it is free of chromatic aberration, a common problem in multi-beam imaging (Theer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the single-beam excitation approach, supported by citation to Theer et al., 2014.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ responses represent a sensitive readout for non-lethal cell stress.
source: Intracellular Ca2+ responses represent a sensitive readout for non-lethal cell stress, caused by opening of calcium channels as well as by transient membrane damage caused by reactive oxygen species and other cytotoxic events (Hopt and Neher, 2001; Iwanaga et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hopt and Neher, 2001 and Iwanaga et al., 2006.

claim: Intermittent highIR scanning at toxic intensity (17 nJ) caused rapid-onset Ca2+ elevation in cell subsets followed by gradual increase of the Sytox signal.
source: As a positive control, intermittent highIR scanning at toxic intensity (17 nJ) caused rapid-onset Ca2+ elevation in cell subsets followed by gradual increase of the Sytox signal (Figure 2b, frames #102–201).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The Ca2+ signal reliably indicated phototoxic stress, prior to detection of cell death by Sytox and even in cells which remained viable at the experimental endpoint.
source: Thus, the Ca2+ signal reliably indicated phototoxic stress, prior to detection of cell death by Sytox and even in cells which remained viable at the experimental endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis of Ca2+ and Sytox responses shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A threshold for excitation energy in the focus of up to 8.4 nJ at the sample surface allows for safe time-lapse imaging inside the tissue, when focusing at least 40 µm deep inside the sample.
source: Thus, a threshold for excitation energy in the focus of up to 8.4 nJ at the sample surface allows for safe time-lapse imaging inside the tissue, when focusing at least 40 µm deep inside the sample.
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Both Ca2+ and Sytox signals were spatially restricted within the highIR excitation plane, without effects in regions above and below.
source: Both Ca2+ and Sytox signals were spatially restricted within the highIR excitation plane, without effects in regions above and below (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by depth-stack measurements shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-f.

claim: Continuous scanning with 1700 nm highIR excitation power of 17 mW (17 nJ × 1 MHz) at the sample surface can be used without causing linear phototoxicity.
source: This result shows that continuous scanning with 1700 nm highIR excitation power of 17 mW (17 nJ × 1 MHz) at the sample surface can be used without causing linear phototoxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial restriction of damage to the focal plane shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-f.

claim: During continuous highIR exposure for energies at the sample surface below or equal to 2.8 nJ (1300 nm) or 8.7 nJ (1650 nm), the Ca2+ signal retained background activity, with occasional spontaneous Ca2+ fluctuations.
source: During continuous highIR exposure for energies at the sample surface below or equal to 2.8 nJ (1300 nm) or 8.7 nJ (1650 nm), the Ca2+ signal retained background activity, with occasional spontaneous Ca2+ fluctuations (Figure 2g, asterisk; Figure 2—videos 1; 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging experiments shown in Figure 2g and associated videos.

claim: Higher excitation energies (3.9 nJ for 1300 nm, 12 nJ for 1650 nm) induced Ca2+ elevation in cell subsets.
source: Higher excitation energies (3.9 nJ for 1300 nm, 12 nJ for 1650 nm) induced Ca2+ elevation in cell subsets (Figure 2g and Figure 2—videos 1; 2, arrowheads).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging experiments shown in Figure 2g and associated videos.

claim: Within the toxic range, eGFP intensity declined by 25% after 25 scans (1300 nm) and mCherry intensity declined by 25% after two scans (1650 nm).
source: Within the toxic range, eGFP intensity declined by 25% after 25 scans (1300 nm) and mCherry intensity declined by 25% after two scans (1650 nm) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Within the non-toxic range, mCherry intensity decreased by 10–20% after 50 scans, while 3P-excited eGFP signal remained stable.
source: Within the non-toxic range, mCherry intensity decreased by 10–20% after 50 scans, while 3P-excited eGFP signal remained stable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: 3P and 4P highIR excitation resolved subcellular features of eGFP and TagRFP labeled cells at depths beyond 400 µm, as compared to 225 µm for OPO-generated 2P lowIR excitation.
source: 3P and 4P highIR excitation resolved subcellular features of eGFP and TagRFP labeled cells at depths beyond 400 µm, as compared to 225 µm for OPO-generated 2P lowIR excitation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging depth comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: While the SNR remained above the detection limit (SNR ≥3) until a depth of only ~255 µm using the 2P lowIR excitation regime, the 3P highIR excitation regime enabled reaching depths of ~395 µm (1650 nm) or ~415 µm (1300 nm).
source: While the SNR remained above the detection limit (SNR ≥3) until a depth of only ~255 µm using the 2P lowIR excitation regime, the 3P highIR excitation regime enabled us to reach depths of ~395 µm (1650 nm) or ~415 µm (1300 nm) (Figure 3c), corresponding to a nearly 2-fold increase as compared to lowIR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SNR analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: For 3PE and 4PE processes, resolution remained higher with increasing imaging depth as compared to the resolution achieved by 2PE, which declined steeply beyond 125 µm.
source: For 3PE and 4PE processes, resolution remained higher with increasing imaging depth as compared to the resolution achieved by 2PE, which declined steeply beyond 125 µm (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by axial resolution analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: When red-shifting the excitation wavelength from 1180 to 1300 or 1650 nm, le increased from 103 to 128 or 220 µm, respectively.
source: When red-shifting the excitation wavelength from 1180 to 1300 or 1650 nm, le increased from 103 to 128 or 220 µm, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by signal attenuation analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: HighIR excitation increases the imaging depth by 2-fold compared to lowIR excitation using OPO-based sources and by 4-fold compared to lowIR excitation in the 800–900 nm range.
source: Through these combined effects, highIR excitation increases the imaging depth by 2-fold compared to lowIR excitation using OPO-based sources and by 4-fold compared to lowIR excitation in the 800–900 nm range (Andresen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of the imaging depth improvements demonstrated throughout the manuscript, with citation to Andresen et al., 2009.

claim: HighIR-excited THG resolved extracellular and cellular details at depths beyond 400 µm in tumor, while lowIR resolved primarily extracellular details until a depth of ~150 µm.
source: In the tumor, highIR-excited THG resolved extracellular and cellular details (arrowheads) at depths beyond 400 µm, while lowIR resolved primarily extracellular details until a depth of ~150 µm (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by THG imaging comparison shown in Figure 4a.

claim: SNR analysis showed a maximum imaging depth of >400 µm for highIR and <100 µm for lowIR in tumor THG imaging.
source: SNR analysis showed a maximum imaging depth of >400 µm for highIR and <100 µm for lowIR (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SNR analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Subcellular structures were reliably resolved by highIR excitation beyond 220 µm depth in bone, including osteocyte lacunae and canaliculi in the cortical bone layer and trabeculae in the bone marrow.
source: Subcellular structures were reliably resolved by highIR excitation beyond 220 µm depth, including osteocyte lacunae and canaliculi in the cortical bone layer and trabeculae in the bone marrow (Figure 4c; yz-projections and arrowheads).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bone imaging shown in Figure 4c.

claim: 1650 nm highIR excitation resulted in both increased effective attenuation length le and larger imaging depth compared to 1270 nm lowIR excitation in bone.
source: In addition, 1650 nm highIR excitation resulted in both increased effective attenuation length le and larger imaging depth compared to 1270 nm lowIR excitation (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by signal attenuation analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The SNR remained above the detection limit up to 928 µm depth for 1650 nm highIR, and up to 444 µm for 1270 nm lowIR excitation in mouse brain.
source: The SNR remained above the detection limit up to 928 µm depth for 1650 nm highIR, and up to 444 µm for 1270 nm lowIR excitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e, dotted lines).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SNR analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claim: The depth gain for THG imaging with highIR was at least 2-fold compared to lowIR excitation and irrespective of tissue type and density, including brain, tumor, and bone.
source: When comparing the applicability of highIR for deep imaging, the depth gain for THG imaging was at least 2-fold compared to lowIR excitation and irrespective of tissue type and density, including brain, tumor, and bone (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the summary of imaging depth limits shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The Ca2+ detection of phototoxic cell stress was faster and more sensitive than recording of irreversible cell death.
source: The Ca2+ detection of phototoxic cell stress was faster and more sensitive than recording of irreversible cell death.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal analysis of Ca2+ and Sytox responses shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The Ca2+ reporter enabled detection of damage which remained sublethal within the time frame of the experiments.
source: Additionally, the Ca2+ reporter enabled to detect damage which remained sublethal within the time frame of the experiments, which may affect cell functionally but could escape detection by commonly used live-death reporters, such as DNA intercalating probes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the observation of Ca2+ responses in cells that remained Sytox-negative, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Cell stress and bleaching were induced in the focal plane when pulse energies reached threshold values (3.9 nJ for 1300 nm and 12 nJ for 1650 nm at 50 µm depth).
source: Cell stress and bleaching were induced in the focal plane when pulse energies reached threshold values (3.9 nJ for 1300 nm and 12 nJ for 1650 nm at 50 µm depth), eventually leading to physical disruption of tissue structures (burning marks), in line with observations by others (Hopt and Neher, 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phototoxicity experiments shown in Figure 2, with citation to Hopt and Neher, 2001.

claim: The in-focus phototoxicity thresholds obtained in the cell-rich tumor model are comparable to the dynamic range detected in low-density tissues.
source: The in-focus phototoxicity thresholds obtained in the cell-rich tumor model are comparable to the dynamic range detected in low-density tissues (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Yildirim et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020), indicating that nonlinear phototoxicity might have a general cause, such as light-induced ionization or formation of reactive oxygen species (Débarre et al., 2014; Tirlapur et al., 2001), irrespective of the tissue density.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited studies and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Up to six-channel multiparametric images were generated in live tumors with sufficient signal-to-noise ratio using a single highIR excitation.
source: We generated up to six-channel multiparametric images in live tumors with sufficient signal-to-noise ratio using a single highIR excitation, simultaneously detecting 3PEF and 4PEF along with SHG and THG (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiparametric imaging shown in Figure 1b and summarized in Figure 5b.

claim: The used excitation pulse energy in the focus was higher compared to previous studies: 1.4–2.1 times for 1650 nm and 0.7–1.7 times for 1300 nm, but still below the defined phototoxicity thresholds.
source: To achieve multiparametric imaging, the used excitation pulse energy in the focus was higher compared to previous studies: 1.4–2.1 times for 1650 nm (Horton et al., 2013; Li et al., 2020; Guesmi et al., 2018) and 0.7–1.7 times for 1300 nm (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018a), but still below the defined phototoxicity thresholds.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited studies and reference to the phototoxicity thresholds established in Figure 2.

claim: The requirements for fluorophore concentration and brightness are stricter for 4P, as compared to 3P excitation processes, due to their even smaller absorption cross-section.
source: On the other hand, the requirements for fluorophore concentration and brightness are stricter for 4P, as compared to 3P excitation processes (Figure 5b), due to their even smaller absorption cross-section (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2014 and summarized in Figure 5b.

claim: Fluorophores with high quantum efficiency and/or abundance, such as H2B/eGFP or Hoechst must be selected for 4P excitation.
source: Therefore, fluorophores with high quantum efficiency and/or abundance, such as H2B/eGFP or Hoechst must be selected for 4P excitation.
evidence: This is inferred from the stricter requirements for 4P excitation and the successful use of these fluorophores in the experiments.

claim: At 1300 nm, red fluorescent proteins were excited with reduced efficiency.
source: At 1300 nm however, red fluorescent proteins were excited with reduced efficiency.
evidence: This is observed in the imaging experiments and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The excitation efficiency of red fluorescent proteins at 1300 nm was enhanced by carefully tuning the central excitation wavelength to higher-energy electronic excited states, enabling multiparametric imaging with high SNR in three fluorescent channels, at the cost of accelerated photobleaching.
source: Recently, the excitation efficiency of red fluorescent proteins at 1300 nm was enhanced by carefully tuning the central excitation wavelength to higher-energy electronic excited states, enabling multiparametric imaging with high SNR in three fluorescent channels, at the cost of accelerated photobleaching (Hontani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hontani et al., 2021.

claim: HighIR excitation has two important advantages in the context of tumor microscopy: it can roughly double the imaging depth compared to previous state-of-the-art 2P imaging, and it gives access to multiparametric imaging through the simultaneous detection of 3- and 4P fluorescence excitation and multi-harmonic signals.
source: HighIR excitation has two important advantages in the context of tumor microscopy: it can roughly double the imaging depth compared to previous state-of-the-art 2P imaging, and it gives access to multiparametric imaging through the simultaneous detection of 3- and 4P fluorescence excitation and multi-harmonic signals (You et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings demonstrated throughout the manuscript, with citation to You et al., 2018b.

claim: HighIR excitation will improve intravital microscopy of understudied regions, including the tumor core and necrosis zones.
source: In cancer research, highIR excitation will improve intravital microscopy of understudied regions, including the tumor core and necrosis zones (Deryugina and Kiosses, 2017).
evidence: This is a prospective claim about future applications, supported by citation to Deryugina and Kiosses, 2017.

claim: HighIR excitation should advance live imaging of structurally challenging tissues, including the bone marrow, organoids, and embryos.
source: Beyond cancer, highIR excitation should advance live imaging of structurally challenging tissues, including the bone marrow (Kim and Bixel, 2020), organoids, and embryos (Débarre et al., 2014; Guesmi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prospective claim about future applications, supported by citations.

claim: The much-improved THG signal, together with SHG, 3- and 4P fluorescence excitation of molecular reporters and/or endogenous fluorophores, will allow to record cell type and dynamic functions in a broader morphological context.
source: In addition, the much-improved THG signal, together with SHG, 3- and 4P fluorescence excitation of molecular reporters and/or endogenous fluorophores, will allow to record cell type and dynamic functions in a broader morphological context (Hontani et al., 2021; You et al., 2018b; Guesmi et al., 2018), such as cell activities and inflammation in the tumor microenvironment and label-free intra-operative histology (You et al., 2018b; You et al., 2018a; Zhang et al., 2019; Weigelin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a prospective claim about future applications, supported by citations.
